In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular basis of nuclear membrane organization in interphase and mitosis.
the molecular mechanisms that govern membrane trafficking and the dynamics of membrane proteins in living cells.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NE in mitotic cells is a highly mobile, interconnected membrane system, with no indication for the formation of vesicles.
nuclear envelope disassembly is a process that occurs in the context of the endoplasmic reticulum, and not as a consequence of its fragmentation.
the inner nuclear membrane is not a stable compartment but a dynamic structure with a high degree of mobility and flexibility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inner nuclear membrane is maintained in a continuous membrane system that extends from the nuclear envelope to the ER.
the nuclear membrane system in interphase and mitosis is a continuous, highly interconnected, dynamic system of ER membranes that is compartmentalized by changes in lateral mobility.
the nuclear envelope (and its inner membrane system) does not fragment into vesicles, as was previously believed, but instead is maintained as a continuous membrane network in mitosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LBR-GFP, a protein that is normally localized in the inner nuclear envelope, is also found in ER membranes and can be used to study the dynamics of the ER membrane system in living cells.
the nuclear membrane is a continuous, highly interconnected membrane structure that is not fragmented during mitosis.
